content.p: On the evening of 6 December 1989, a 25-year-old man walked through the École Polytechnique, the engineering school of the Université de Montréal, with a rifle, and shot at women. By the time he killed himself, 14 women were dead and 14 other people were injured, according to the coroner's findings as quoted by Canadian Press. Canadian Press added that the dead were all young women, as were ten of the wounded. The attacker, Marc Lépine, left a letter blaming feminists for ruining his life. The killings became known as the Montreal Massacre, and they remained Canada's largest mass murder until the Nova Scotia killings of 2020, according to Canadian Press.

The attack changed how Canadian police respond to a gunman inside a building, fed a long fight over firearms law, and gave Canada a national day of remembrance. What it meant has been argued over ever since.
content.h2: Four o'clock to ten past five
content.p: The coroner's report, quoted at length by Canadian Press on the 35th anniversary, places Lépine in the school's registrar's office between about 4:00 and 4:40 p.m. He was seen rummaging in a green plastic bag. He did not speak to anyone. When an employee at the counter asked whether she could help him, he gave no answer and left.

At 5:10 p.m. he walked into a mechanical engineering classroom, holding a rifle. A student was giving a presentation. The coroner recorded that, according to the school's computer file, as many as 69 students and two professors could have been in the room. Lépine fired a shot at the ceiling and ordered the room to separate, the women to one side and the men to the other. Nobody moved at first. He repeated the order more sharply, and the students shuffled into groups. Told that the men should leave, they thought it was an end-of-term joke and that the gun held blanks.

Nine women were left standing at the back, with no exit. Lépine asked if they knew why they were there. One of them said no. "I am fighting feminism," he replied. The student who had spoken, Nathalie Provost, answered that they were not feminists and had never fought against men. Lépine began shooting from left to right. After perhaps 30 shots he left the room. Nine women had been hit and six of them died.

The coroner's list of the six dead in that room, each a mechanical engineering student, was Annie St-Arneault (23), Sonia Pelletier (28), Anne-Marie Lemay (22), Barbara Daigneault (22), Nathalie Croteau (23) and Hélène Colgan (23). Provost survived. Two days later she was wheeled on a hospital bed into a press conference, having been shot four times, and told reporters she felt very lucky. She said the gunman started shooting without answering her. "Everybody did their best; that's the essential thing," she said. "There's only one culprit and he's dead."

From there the report follows Lépine corridor by corridor. He shot at two people in a photocopier room and wounded another student on the way. He went into another classroom, aimed at a woman at the back and tried twice to fire, but the weapon did not work. A student coming down an emergency staircase met him face to face and heard him say he was out of bullets, then bumped into him and ran. Lépine reloaded, fired three shots into the locked door of a classroom without getting in, and wounded a woman in the foyer who got up and fled to the fifth floor.

At the finance office, a young woman locked the door as he ran toward her. He fired through the window of the door. The woman at the door was Maryse Laganière, 25, who worked in the finance department. Canadian Press, quoting the coroner, says she was the one victim who was not a student.

He then went down to the cafeteria on the first floor, where about 100 people were present. He shot Barbara Klucznik-Widajewicz near the kitchens; she was 31 and studying nursing, and was the eldest of the 14. Most people in the cafeteria left as the first shots rang out. In an unlocked storage area at the far end he fired on two students and both died: Geneviève Bergeron, 21, who studied mechanical engineering, and Anne-Marie Edward, also 21, who studied chemical engineering. He told a man and a woman hiding under a table to get out, and they were not shot.

On the third floor, in a materials engineering class, he ordered three students giving a presentation to get out and fired at a student on the platform. Two women trying to escape through the front door were wounded and died: Maud Haviernick, 29, and Michèle Richard, 21, both metallurgical engineering students. He then fired on people hiding among the desks, hitting four, one of whom died. She was Annie Turcotte, a metallurgical engineering student whose age the coroner gave as 20.

The student he had shot first on the platform asked for help. Lépine went to her and stabbed her three times with a knife. She was Maryse Leclair, 23, also a metallurgical engineering student. Her father was a Montreal police officer who answered the shooting call and found her body, according to Canadian Press.

Lépine then put the knife down on the instructor's desk, sat on the platform, wrapped his coat around the barrel of the rifle and shot himself. According to the coroner, he still had 60 unused bullets. In the words of the Canadian Press retelling, he was not pinned down or surrounded and no tactical team was approaching. The coroner's study found that all those who died did so because of the severity of their injuries and that none could have survived.

Sources differ on some details. The Canadian Encyclopedia counts 13 wounded rather than 14, while EBSCO says approximately a dozen. Global News says he shot or stabbed 27 people in all. Ages differ too: EBSCO gives Lemay as 27 and Turcotte as 21, against the coroner's 22 and 20. Global News and CBC give the length of the attack as 20 minutes, the coroner's account as 19.

Genevieve Cauden was in a classroom that Lépine entered. She told CBC's As It Happens the following day that those present first took the shots for a joke, until a man came in and told them it was real. Everyone got on the floor and under the desks. She said she closed her eyes and ears, and was hit in the head. "I don't know why in that classroom," she said, "I don't know why in that school and I don't know why then." She recalled that the class held eight women, and that four of her friends were dead.

Outside, the scene was chaotic. Canadian Press wrote that officers arrived but held off entering until backup came, with word going round that there might be several gunmen, and that ambulances were kept back. Students waited in the snow. Parents arrived on hearing of the shooting on the radio and tried to push through the crowd.

A handwritten three-page letter was found in Lépine's jacket, and two letters to friends were recovered later, all dated 6 December 1989, according to the coroner. The coroner wrote that in two of the documents Lépine named feminists as the enemy and that he called suicide his main motive, describing the killings as an extended suicide. One line of the letter, as quoted by Canadian Press, reads, "I decided to send Ad Patres the feminists who have always ruined my life." A list of 19 Quebec women he regarded as radical feminists was attached; the Canadian Encyclopedia says it included journalists, television personalities and union leaders. Another sentence in the letter said that "the lack of time" had allowed them to survive.

Police would not release the letter. Journalist Francine Pelletier, who was named on the list, lobbied for it and was repeatedly denied, until a copy came to her anonymously before the first anniversary. La Presse published it in December 1990, according to Canadian Press.

The coroner described a man of medium size, closed and unsociable except when talking about computers, who did not accept authority and planned everything in detail. He had a stable job until September 1988. In 1986 he had applied to the engineering faculty and was admitted on condition that he complete two courses; he completed the chemistry one in 1989. Global News called him a student who had been rejected and blamed women for that failure. The Action on Armed Violence charity wrote instead that he was never a student at the school, although the coroner found him very familiar with the campus. Those accounts do not agree. In September 1989 he applied to the Sûreté du Québec for a firearms acquisition permit and was granted it. The coroner records that he bought the rifle on 21 November 1989. Under the law then in force, Action on Armed Violence says, applicants for the certificate had no training requirement, and a firearm did not have to be registered.

The Canadian Encyclopedia says the aftermath divided opinion. For some, Lépine's act was an isolated one with no social meaning; for others it revealed a deep malaise about women's place in society. EBSCO describes two lenses in the media: one treated it as a symptom of social attitudes toward women, the other concentrated on the killer's psychology and a childhood in which he suffered abuse. EBSCO also reports that some coverage blamed the school's male students for not protecting their classmates, and that this harmed survivors. Heidi Rathjen, a Polytechnique graduate who was in a nearby study room that night, has called the shooting a femicide. In 2019 a plaque in a memorial park, which had called the shooting a "tragic event", was changed to say "anti-feminist attack" (Canadian Press).

Michèle Thibodeau-DeGuire, the school's head of communications in 1989 and later chair of its board, told CBC in 2021 that it is crucial to call the shooting a femicide: "Once you name them, you know what you're going after."

In 1989, according to Global News, police protocol called for officers to set up a perimeter and not enter until it was confirmed that Lépine had shot himself. Coroner Teresa Sourour noted that he could have killed more people while police waited outside. Global News reports that the attack brought changes in police protocol, credited with limiting casualties at Dawson College in September 2006, where officers went straight in. That attack killed one person before the gunman killed himself.

The firearms campaign began among the students. According to Rathjen, they launched a nationwide petition and counted signatures late into the night. They first sought a ban on all semi-automatic rifles, but when they realised it would catch many legitimate hunting rifles, they asked instead for a ban on "military and paramilitary weapons", a term the RCMP preferred then, according to the Globe and Mail. Action on Armed Violence says the newly formed Canadians for Gun Control later merged with Polytechnique students to form the Coalition for Gun Control.

Bill C-17 passed in 1991, banned high-capacity magazines for automatic and semi-automatic firearms, imposed a 28-day waiting period for a certificate, and required a photograph and two references. From 1994 applicants had to complete a safety course. The Coalition said it did not go far enough. The Firearms Act, which came into force in 1995 according to Action on Armed Violence (the Canadian Encyclopedia dates Bill C-68 to November 1995), created a firearms registry and required licences for gun owners. The Globe and Mail adds that magazines were limited to five rounds and that models "not reasonably used in hunting" were restricted or prohibited. The registration requirements were dropped in 2012 with Bill C-19, and the Harper government scrapped the long-gun registry. The list of prohibited models, the Globe and Mail says, was not updated as new models arrived.

The Ruger Mini-14 remained legal. In 1999, justice minister Anne McLellan said the Chrétien government would prohibit it once the long-gun registry was "satisfactorily implemented", the Globe reported; that never happened. In 2019, Edward Burlew, a lawyer who works on firearms cases with pro-gun groups, called it "a very fine hunting rifle". Provost responded: "A vermin gun? We were not vermin 30 years ago." The Liberal government had just promised to ban "military-style assault rifles", and Rathjen predicted the Mini-14 would be included.

In 1991 Parliament declared 6 December the National Day of Remembrance and Action on Violence Against Women, according to the Canadian Encyclopedia. On the 32nd anniversary in 2021, a wreath was laid at the university and, in the evening, 14 beams of light were projected into the sky from Mount Royal. Serge St-Arneault, a brother of Annie St-Arneault and a member of the gun-control group PolySeSouvient, said the gunman "had disfigured the face of humanity where each person is a sacred story". The same CBC report said some 2,000 women at Polytechnique now study to become engineers. Provost, described at the 25th anniversary by Canadian Press as a mother of four working for the Quebec government, said in 2021 that Canada must keep fighting for better gun control.
